title: Double treble — the tall stitch for lace and openwork
subtitle: Two yarn-overs on entry, three yarn-overs to close — the lace stitch of Victorian crochet
excerpt: Double treble (UK dtr) is the tall stitch used in lace borders, shawl edgings, and open crochet panels. Two yarn-overs before inserting, then three close stages. US patterns call it treble crochet.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — the double treble in lace and edging work. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 3 (1888) — double treble in open mesh patterns.

glossaryTerms.definition: UK term for a tall crochet stitch with two yarn-overs on entry: yarn over twice, insert hook, pull up loop (four loops on hook), then yarn over and pull through two loops three times. US patterns call this treble crochet.

content.text: is one step taller than the treble. Two yarn-overs before inserting the hook, four loops on the hook after pulling up, and three sequential closes to finish. The stitch is tall, open, and drapes well — it appears in lace edgings, shawl borders, and open-mesh stitch patterns. US patterns call it treble crochet (tr).
Chain 15. The turning chain for dtr is ch 4, which counts as the first double treble.
Row 1: ch 4 (counts as first dtr). Yarn over twice, then insert hook into the 5th chain from the hook.
Yarn over and pull up a loop — four loops on the hook.
Yarn over and pull through the first two loops — three loops remain.
Yarn over and pull through the next two loops — two loops remain.
Yarn over and pull through the final two loops. One dtr made.
Work 1 dtr in each chain across — 12 dtr including the ch-4. Turn.
Row 2: ch 4 (counts as first dtr), skip the first stitch. Work 1 dtr across. Last dtr into the top of the ch-4 from the previous row. 12 dtr. Turn.
Where double treble appears in patterns

Double treble works into chain spaces in lace edgings, creating tall arched shapes. Crossed double treble pairs are worked in reverse order to make X-shapes in Victorian open-lace panels. In motif patterns, a group of dtr can form a fan shape or a shell taller than anything a treble achieves.

items.symptom: Losing track of which loop-pair to close
items.cause: Counting loops is harder with four on the hook
items.fix: Close from the tip of the hook down — always pull through the two loops nearest the tip first, then the next two, then the last two. The rule is always 'two at a time, tip first'.

items.cause: The yarn-over loops from before inserting are placed at different heights on the hook
items.fix: Make both entry yarn-overs at the same position on the shaft, not one high and one low. They should look like identical size loops before you insert.

content.text: Triple treble (three entry yarn-overs) extends the same logic one step further and is used in hairpin lace and deep lace arches. Crossed double treble works two dtr in reverse order to make a taller X-stitch for lace panels.
